text: Castellan Retail runs a public order-tracking storefront, a staff office, a small server room, and guest Wi-Fi, all on one flat network today, with the public web server sharing a subnet with the payroll file share. This lab redesigns that layout from scratch using nothing but Chapter 1's firewall and segmentation concepts, applied to one real company.

The design starts with a single perimeter firewall holding three interfaces instead of two: WAN facing the ISP, a DMZ, and the internal network. That's the three-legged firewall layout from Lesson 3, with one device enforcing the boundary between all three zones instead of pretending a public web server and payroll data deserve equal trust.

The order-tracking web server moves into the DMZ, alone with its reverse proxy. Only two rules govern traffic from the internet: allow tcp 80 and 443 to that one web server, deny everything else to the DMZ. A server the public can reach is assumed reachable by an attacker eventually, so it's isolated with no direct path to anything else.

The internal network splits into three VLANs trunked off the core switch: Workstations for staff machines, Servers for the file server, domain controller, and internal order database, and Guest Wi-Fi for visitors. A compromised workstation should never be one hop from the domain controller, and a guest device should never be one hop from either.

The web server needs some internal data, which is where flat designs usually undo their own DMZ. The fix is narrow on every axis: one rule allowing the DMZ web server to reach one internal database host on one port, and a second rule denying everything else from the DMZ to the internal network — host to host, not subnet to subnet.

Guest Wi-Fi gets a rule permitting outbound internet access and an explicit deny to every internal VLAN in both directions, because a guest network isn't a weaker internal network — it has no internal route at all. Next up, Chapter 2's rule syntax gets turned loose on a real, specific attack pattern.
